It elevates the earlier Directive Principle (Article 45) into a justiciable Fundamental Right.

content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 21A of the Constitution of India provides that the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine. It was inserted by the Constitution (Eighty-Sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, and is the constitutional foundation of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act).

Constitutional Journey
1. Original Article 45 (DPSP): The State shall endeavour to provide free and compulsory education for all children until they complete the age of fourteen years.
2. Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) and Unni Krishnan v. State of A.P. (1993): The Supreme Court read a right to education into Article 21, holding that education up to the age of 14 is a Fundamental Right flowing from the right to life.
3. 86th Amendment (2002):
   - Inserted Article 21A (justiciable right for ages 6–14).
   - Amended Article 45 to focus on early childhood care and education for children below six years.
   - Added Article 51A(k) — duty of parents/guardians to provide educational opportunities to children aged 6–14.
4. RTE Act, 2009: Statutory implementation — free and compulsory education, 25% reservation in private unaided schools for children from disadvantaged groups and weaker sections, norms for schools, teachers, and curriculum.

Scope of Article 21A
1. Age band: 6 to 14 years (not 0–6 or post-14 as a constitutional right under 21A itself).
2. “Free”: No fee, charge or expense that prevents the child from pursuing elementary education.
3. “Compulsory”: Obligation on the State to ensure admission, attendance and completion; corresponding duty on parents under Article 51A(k).
4. “In such manner as the State may, by law, determine”: Parliament and State Legislatures have leeway on the design of the scheme, subject to the core guarantee.

Private Institutions and Article 21A / RTE
1. Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012): The 25% reservation under Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act was upheld for private unaided non-minority schools; minority institutions under Article 30 were held exempt.
2. Pramati Educational & Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014): Confirmed that the RTE Act (including the 25% quota) does not apply to minority educational institutions, whether aided or unaided, protected under Article 30(1).

Relationship with Article 21
Article 21A is a specific embodiment of the broader right to education recognised under Article 21 in Unni Krishnan. Post-86th Amendment, the 6–14 right is textually anchored in 21A; education beyond that age continues to draw support from Article 21 and Directive Principles, but is not a free-standing justiciable right of the same intensity.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors
1. Forum: Article 32 / 226 for enforcement of the right and challenge to non-implementation; statutory remedies under the RTE Act (local authorities, State commissions, National Commission for Protection of Child Rights).
2. Standing: Child, parent/guardian, NGO, or public-spirited citizen.
3. Typical directions: Ensure admission, free textbooks and uniforms, appointment of teachers, compliance with pupil–teacher ratio, enforcement of 25% quota in non-minority private schools.
4. Evidence: Enrolment and attendance data, school recognition records, notifications under the RTE Act, affidavits of denial of admission.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Article 21A is in force. The RTE Act, 2009 (as amended) is the primary implementing statute. Minority institutions remain outside the 25% quota mandate (Pramati). Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Denial of Free Admission (Applies)
examples.body: A government school demands a “development fee” from a child in Class IV as a condition of continued enrolment. This violates the “free” component of Article 21A and the RTE Act. The fee demand is unconstitutional and illegal.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Minority Institution Exemption (Does Not Attract 25% Quota)
examples.body: A minority educational institution protected under Article 30(1) refuses to implement the 25% RTE quota. Under Pramati, the institution is exempt. Article 21A does not override the minority right in this respect.

hypotheticals.question: Examine the constitutional validity of the school’s refusal in light of Article 21A and the RTE Act.
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Article 21A obliges the State to provide free and compulsory education; the RTE Act is the chosen manner of implementation.
2. Section 12(1)(c) mandates 25% reservation in private unaided schools; the Supreme Court upheld this for non-minority institutions.
3. Article 19(1)(g) is subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public; the quota is a reasonable restriction serving the constitutional right to education.
4. Financial hardship may entitle the school to reimbursement as provided under the RTE Act, but does not justify outright refusal.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain Article 21A of the Constitution. How is the right to free and compulsory education implemented?
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE
Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14.

II. CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT AND HISTORY
Inserted by the 86th Amendment (2002) after Mohini Jain and Unni Krishnan read education into Article 21. Article 45 was recast for early childhood; Article 51A(k) added a parental duty.

III. IMPLEMENTATION — RTE ACT, 2009
The Act provides free and compulsory elementary education, school norms, and a 25% reservation in private unaided non-minority schools for disadvantaged groups and weaker sections. Minority institutions are exempt (Pramati).

IV. ENFORCEMENT
Writ jurisdiction under Articles 32/226; statutory authorities under the RTE Act.

V. CONCLUSION
Article 21A converts a Directive Principle into a justiciable Fundamental Right for the 6–14 age group. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.question: Critically examine the right to education under Article 21A. Discuss its relationship with Article 21, the RTE Act, and the rights of minority educational institutions.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION
Article 21A is the express constitutional guarantee of free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen. It sits at the intersection of the right to life, social justice Directive Principles, and institutional autonomy claims of private and minority schools.

II. FROM DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLE TO FUNDAMENTAL RIGHT
Original Article 45 directed the State to provide free and compulsory education up to age 14. Mohini Jain and Unni Krishnan elevated education to a Fundamental Right under Article 21. The 86th Amendment crystallised the 6–14 segment in Article 21A, shifted early childhood to Article 45, and added a parental duty under Article 51A(k).

III. SCOPE OF ARTICLE 21A
The right is age-specific (6–14), free of cost barriers, and compulsory on the State. The phrase “in such manner as the State may, by law, determine” gives legislative flexibility but does not dilute the core entitlement.

IV. RTE ACT AND PRIVATE SCHOOLS
Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act mandates 25% reservation in private unaided schools. The Supreme Court in Society for Unaided Private Schools upheld this for non-minority institutions as a reasonable restriction on Article 19(1)(g). Pramati Educational & Cultural Trust held that minority institutions under Article 30(1) are exempt from the RTE Act’s quota and related obligations that would abrogate their minority character.

V. ARTICLE 21A AND ARTICLE 21
Article 21A is a specific, textually anchored right. Article 21 continues to support a broader educational dimension (dignity, development, higher education access) but without the same free-and-compulsory mandate for ages outside 6–14.

VI. LITIGATION STRATEGY
1. For denial of free elementary education: plead Article 21A + RTE Act; seek mandamus for admission and facilities.
2. For quota disputes: identify whether the institution is minority-protected; if not, the 25% mandate applies.
3. Evidence: age proof, residence, income/disadvantage certificates, school recognition status.

VII. CONCLUSION
Article 21A is a landmark social right. Its effectiveness depends on statutory implementation, judicial enforcement, and careful balancing with minority rights under Article 30. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

essentialIngredients: Target Age Group: Applies strictly to children between the age of six (6) and fourteen (14) years.

Dual Obligation: Must provide both 'free' education (no child liable to pay any fee or charges preventing completion of elementary education) and 'compulsory' education (binding duty on the State to ensure admission, attendance, and completion).
Manner Determined by Law: The phrase 'in such manner as the State may, by law, determine' left the operational roadmap to Parliament, leading to the enactment of the RTE Act, 2009.

25% Economically Weaker Section Quota: Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act mandates non-minority private schools to reserve at least 25% of their entry-level seats for children from disadvantaged groups and weaker sections.
Exclusion of Minority Institutions: Does not apply to minority educational institutions protected under Article 30(1) (Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India).
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Article 21A is one of the greatest transformative achievements in Indian constitutional history.

### 1. The Judicial Genesis
Originally, education was situated in Part IV under **Article 45** as a non-justiciable Directive Principle.
- **Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992):** The Supreme Court held that the 'right to education' is directly emanative from the right to life under Article 21, and struck down exorbitant 'capitation fees' charged by private medical colleges.
- **Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993):** A 5-judge Constitution Bench tempered Mohini Jain, holding that every child has a fundamental right to free education until they complete the age of 14 years, after which the right is circumscribed by the economic capacity and development of the State.

### 2. The 86th Constitutional Amendment, 2002
In response to Unni Krishnan, Parliament enacted the 86th Amendment, creating a tripartite constitutional architecture:
1. Inserted **Article 21A** in Part III (Fundamental Right for ages 6–14);
2. Substituted **Article 45** in Part IV (Directive Principle for early childhood care below age 6);
3. Added Clause (k) to **Article 51A** in Part IVA (Fundamental Duty of parents/guardians to provide educational opportunities).

### 3. The RTE Act & The Private School Quota Controversy
The Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010. Section 12(1)(c) mandated private unaided schools to admit at least 25% students from weaker sections, with the State reimbursing tuition costs.
In *Society for Unaided Private Schools of India v. Union of India (2012)* and *Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust (2014)*, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Section 12(1)(c), holding that it does not infringe the freedom of trade under Article 19(1)(g), but clarified that minority schools (aided or unaided) are exempt under Article 30(1).
examples: Enforcement of 25% Quota in Private Schools: An elite private unaided school refuses admission to an orphaned child living in an adjacent slum who applied under the 25% EWS quota. On an Article 226 petition, the High Court issues a writ of mandamus directing the school to admit the child and provide free uniforms and textbooks pursuant to Article 21A and Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act.

Denial of Admission for Lack of Birth Certificate: A municipal school turns away an 8-year-old child of migrant construction workers because the parents lack a formal municipal birth certificate. The High Court holds the denial unconstitutional: under Article 21A and the RTE Act, lack of age documentation cannot be used to deny admission to elementary education.
distinctions: Article 21A vs Article 45: Article 21A is an enforceable Fundamental Right in Part III for children aged 6 to 14 years; Article 45 is a non-justiciable Directive Principle in Part IV directing the State to provide early childhood care and education to children below 6 years.

Article 21A vs Article 51A(k): Article 21A imposes a binding legal obligation on the State to provide free education; Article 51A(k) creates a moral fundamental duty on parents or guardians to provide educational opportunities to their wards.
problemApplication: Issue: A private non-minority school refuses to admit 25% students from economically weaker sections under Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act, contending that compelling it to provide free seats violates its fundamental right to carry on an occupation under Article 19(1)(g). Is the school's contention legally tenable?

Rule: The Supreme Court in Society for Unaided Private Schools and Pramati held that Article 21A and Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act are constitutionally valid and represent a reasonable restriction on Article 19(1)(g).
Application: Education is a public duty, not mere commerce. Private schools receive state recognition and function within a constitutional ecosystem where child rights under Article 21A prevail.
Counterargument: The school contends that the State must build its own public schools rather than burden private enterprise.
Conclusion: The school's contention is legally untenable. It is bound by Article 21A and Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act, subject to statutory tuition reimbursement by the State.
